_source: Company tags come from public candidate reports (systemdesign.io question list, Oct 2026). Empty means no public source yet.

reqF: Shorten a long URL to a 7-character code
Redirect a code to the original URL
reqN: Very read heavy: 100 reads per write
Highly available: a dead link is a broken promise
est: Writes: 100M/day ≈ 1,200/s, peaks ~5k/s
Reads: 100x ≈ 120k/s, peaks ~500k/s
Storage: 100M x 500 B x 365 x 5 yr ≈ 90 TB
Cache: top 20% of daily reads ≈ a few hundred GB
data: urls: code PK, long_url, user_id, created_at, expires_at
Key-value store partitioned by code
clicks: append-only events to Kafka, rolled up in the warehouse

blocks.u: Start from the people clicking links: almost all traffic is redirects.
blocks.lb: Spreads redirect traffic across stateless API servers.
blocks.api: Stateless service: creates codes and serves redirects.
blocks.id: Hands out unique 64-bit ids; base62 of the id is the code, so no collisions.
blocks.c: Hot codes live in Redis: most redirects never touch the DB.
blocks.db: Key-value store, partitioned by code: one lookup per miss.
blocks.k: Click events go to a queue so redirects stay fast.
blocks.w: Analytics runs offline on the warehouse, not on the hot path.

dives: How do you generate codes without collisions?
A Snowflake-style id generator, then base62. 7 chars = 3.5 trillion codes. No check-and-retry needed.
301 is cached by browsers (fewer hits, no click tracking). 302 every time (lets you count clicks).
How do you keep redirects under 50 ms?
Cache hot codes (80/20 rule), CDN or edge for the top links, KV store sharded by code.
Custom aliases?
Check-and-set insert on the alias; reject if taken.
wrap: Bottleneck: the KV store on cache misses. Fix: bigger cache, read replicas.
Abuse: rate limit creation per user, scan for malicious URLs.
Next: expiry cleanup job, analytics dashboards.

reqF: Limit requests per user, IP or API key
Return 429 with Retry-After when over the limit
reqN: Fails open if the limiter is down
est: 1M requests/s at the edge
10M active keys x ~100 B ≈ 1 GB of counters
One Redis round trip per request: shard Redis by key
data: counters in Redis: key = rule:user:window → count, TTL
rules: id, match (path, method), limit, window, scope

blocks.u: Clients of every kind hit one front door.
blocks.gw: The limiter lives in the gateway so every service is protected.
blocks.s: Allowed requests pass straight to the services.
blocks.r: Shared counters in Redis, updated atomically with a Lua script.
blocks.cfg: Rules come from config, so limits change without a deploy.
blocks.x: Over the limit: 429 plus Retry-After, so clients back off.

dives: Which algorithm?
Token bucket: allows short bursts, simple, most common. Sliding window counter if you need smoother limits.
How do you stay correct across many gateways?
Central Redis with an atomic Lua script (INCR + check + EXPIRE in one step).
What if Redis is down?
Fail open with a local in-memory fallback limit, and alert.
Hot keys?
Shard counters by key; keep a local token cache for very hot clients.
wrap: Bottleneck: Redis round trip. Fix: local batching, shard by key.
Next: per-plan limits, dashboards of who is throttled.

reqN: Delivery under 200 ms when both are online
Messages never lost, kept in order per chat
est: 500M DAU x 40 msgs ≈ 20B msgs/day ≈ 230k/s
Storage: 20B x 100 B ≈ 2 TB/day
Open connections: ~100M at peak, ~50k per server ≈ 2k servers
data: messages: chat_id (partition), msg_id (sort), sender, body, ts
chats + members tables
presence in Redis with TTL heartbeats

blocks.a: User A on a phone with a long-lived connection.
blocks.b: User B, maybe on another server or offline.
blocks.w1: WebSocket servers keep open connections for 2-way realtime.
blocks.w2: Each user is pinned to one chat server.
blocks.k: The queue routes messages between servers and absorbs bursts.
blocks.p: Presence lives in Redis with heartbeats and TTLs.
blocks.db: Cassandra: partition by chat, sort by message id, fast writes.
blocks.push: Offline users get a push, then sync when they reconnect.
blocks.s3: Media goes to object storage and a CDN, not through chat servers.

dives: How do you keep order?
Per-chat sequence ids assigned on write; clients sort by them.
How do you avoid duplicates?
Client message id = idempotency key; server dedupes.
Group chat with 500 members?
Fan out through the queue; big groups use pull on open.
How do you know who is online?
Heartbeats every ~30 s into Redis with a TTL.
wrap: Bottleneck: connection servers. Fix: scale horizontally, a registry of user → server.
Next: end-to-end encryption, message search.

reqF: See a feed of people you follow, newest or ranked
reqN: A new post can take a few seconds to appear
est: Reads: 300M x 10 feed loads ≈ 35k/s
Writes: 300M x 0.5 posts ≈ 1.7k/s
Fan-out: avg 200 followers ≈ 350k feed inserts/s
data: posts: post_id, author_id, body, media, created_at
follows: follower_id, followee_id
feed cache: user_id → list of post ids

blocks.u: Readers open the feed far more than they post.
blocks.gw: Auth and routing for posts and feed reads.
blocks.k: New-post events decouple writing from fan-out.
blocks.fo: Workers push the post id into each follower's feed.
blocks.g: Who follows whom, read by the fan-out workers.
blocks.fc: Each feed is a Redis list of post ids, ready to read.
blocks.cdn: Images and video come from the CDN.

dives: Fan-out on write or read?
Write for most users (fast reads). Read-time pull for celebrities. Merge both: hybrid.
Why store ids, not posts, in the feed?
Small lists; hydrate post details from cache at read time.
Pagination?
Cursor based (last post id), never offset.
Ranking?
A ranking service scores candidates; start with recency.
wrap: Bottleneck: fan-out for big accounts. Fix: hybrid fan-out.
Next: ranking model, ads insertion, notifications.

reqF: Watch with smooth playback on any device
reqN: Huge egress: CDN serves almost everything
est: Uploads: 500 hours per minute
Each video stored in ~6 renditions ≈ 5x raw size
Egress: millions of concurrent streams x ~5 Mbps ≈ Tbps, so CDN
data: videos: id, owner, title, status, renditions
segments in object storage: /video/rendition/segment.ts

blocks.up: Hands out pre-signed URLs so uploads go straight to storage.
blocks.raw: Raw uploads land in object storage.
blocks.q: Each upload becomes a transcode job.
blocks.tr: Workers split, encode many bitrates and merge.
blocks.cdn: The CDN serves the bytes, close to viewers.
blocks.v: Viewers stream segments and switch quality on the fly.
blocks.api: Video API serves the watch page and manifest.
blocks.meta: Metadata DB: titles, status, view counts.

dives: Why pre-signed uploads?
Big files skip your servers; resumable multipart upload to S3.
Adaptive bitrate?
Client picks the next segment's quality from measured bandwidth.
How do you transcode fast?
Split into chunks, encode in parallel as a DAG, merge.
Cost of egress?
CDN with high hit ratio, pre-warm popular videos at the edge.
wrap: Bottleneck: transcode backlog. Fix: autoscale workers, prioritise popular creators.
Next: recommendations, live streaming.

reqF: Pay at the end of the trip
reqN: A driver is never offered two trips at once
est: Location writes: 1M / 4 s = 250k/s
Ride requests: ~1k/s at peak
Location data is small and short-lived: keep it in memory
api: WS: driver location updates, ride status pushes
data: trips: id, rider, driver, status, route, fare
driver locations: in-memory geo index (H3 / geohash)

blocks.r: Riders request trips and watch the car arrive.
blocks.d: Drivers stream their location every few seconds.
blocks.t: Trip service owns the ride lifecycle.
blocks.l: Location service ingests 250k updates per second.
blocks.m: Matching finds and locks the best nearby driver.
blocks.geo: In-memory geo index for nearby search.
blocks.tdb: Trips DB: durable record of every ride.
blocks.maps: Maps and ETA service for routes and arrival times.
blocks.pay: Payment runs when the trip ends.

dives: Why not store locations in a database?
250k writes/s of data that expires in seconds: keep it in memory (Redis GEO / H3 cells).
How do you find nearby drivers?
Look up the rider's cell and its neighbours, then rank by ETA.
How do you avoid double booking a driver?
Lock the driver (atomic set with TTL) while the offer is open.
What if a region's servers fail?
Partition by city; failover per region.
wrap: Bottleneck: location ingest. Fix: shard by geo cell.
Next: surge pricing, pooled rides.

reqN: One slow channel never blocks the others
est: 10M/day ≈ 120/s average, bursts 10k/s
Device tokens: 1B x 100 B ≈ 100 GB
data: preferences: user, channel, opt_in, quiet_hours
device_tokens: user, platform, token
log: id, status, timestamps

blocks.s: Any service can trigger a notification.
blocks.n: One service validates, applies preferences and renders templates.
blocks.pref: Preferences and device tokens decide where it can go.
blocks.tpl: Templates keep copy out of code.
blocks.q1: A queue per channel isolates failures.
blocks.q3: SMS is slow and costly, so it is isolated.
blocks.w: Workers send, retry with backoff, then DLQ.

dives: How do you avoid duplicates?
Idempotency key per notification; workers check before sending.
What if a provider is down?
Retry with backoff, then dead-letter queue; failover to a second provider.
Quiet hours?
Delay into a scheduled queue by user time zone.
Rate limits?
Per-user caps so nobody gets spammed.
wrap: Bottleneck: provider limits. Fix: per-channel throttling, multiple providers.
Next: digesting, A/B tests on copy.

reqF: Crawl the web from seed URLs
Re-crawl pages to keep them fresh
reqN: Robust to traps and bad HTML
est: 400 pages/s x 500 KB ≈ 200 MB/s download
Storage: 1B x 500 KB ≈ 500 TB/month (compress)
URL frontier: billions of URLs on disk
data: url seen set (Bloom filter + store)
content: url hash → compressed HTML in S3
frontier: priority queues per host

blocks.seed: Start from a list of seed URLs.
blocks.f: The frontier decides what to fetch next, by priority and politeness.
blocks.dns: A cached DNS resolver avoids a slow lookup per page.
blocks.cs: Raw pages go to object storage.
blocks.dd: A Bloom filter drops URLs already seen.
blocks.seen: The durable set of seen URLs.

dives: How are you polite?
One queue per host, a delay between requests, obey robots.txt.
Duplicates?
URL dedupe with a Bloom filter; content dedupe with simhash.
Crawler traps?
Max depth, URL length limits, per-site page caps.
Freshness?
Re-crawl by page change rate and importance.
wrap: Bottleneck: DNS and network. Fix: DNS cache, more fetchers per region.
Next: JavaScript rendering, ranking signals.

reqN: Never lose a payment: strong consistency
Reconciled with the provider every day
est: 1M payments/day ≈ 12/s average, 100x peaks on sale days
Small data, high stakes: correctness over speed
data: payments: id, order_id, amount, status (state machine), idempotency_key UNIQUE
ledger_entries: account, debit, credit, payment_id (append-only)

blocks.co: Checkout creates the order and calls payments.
blocks.pdb: Payments DB holds the state machine.
blocks.wh: Webhooks confirm results from the provider.
blocks.led: Double-entry ledger: every debit has a credit.
blocks.rec: Daily reconciliation against the provider's settlement file.

dives: How do you never charge twice?
Idempotency key with a UNIQUE constraint; retries return the first result.
What states can a payment be in?
CREATED → PENDING → SUCCEEDED / FAILED, only forward.
Why a ledger?
Append-only double-entry: balances always add up and are auditable.
What if the webhook never arrives?
Poll the provider for pending payments; reconcile daily.
wrap: Bottleneck: provider latency. Fix: async confirmation via webhooks.
Next: multi-currency, payouts, chargebacks.

reqF: Show top 5 suggestions as the user types
reqN: Suggestions can be an hour stale
est: 10B queries x ~5 keystrokes ≈ 600k lookups/s
Unique prefixes: hundreds of millions; top-k cached per prefix fits in memory per shard
data: trie: prefix → top-k completions (in memory, snapshot to store)
query logs → hourly counts

blocks.tc: In-memory trie with top-k cached at each node.
blocks.ts: Trie snapshots in storage, loaded at start.
blocks.log: Every query is logged to a stream.
blocks.tb: Builds a fresh trie offline and swaps it in.

dives: Why cache top-k per node?
Lookup becomes O(prefix length), no tree walk at query time.
How do you update?
Rebuild offline from logs and swap atomically.
Scale?
Shard by prefix range; replicate hot shards.
Client tricks?
Debounce typing, cache in the browser.
wrap: Bottleneck: hot prefixes like 'a'. Fix: replicate, cache at the edge.
Next: personalisation, multiple languages.

est: 50M users x 10 GB ≈ 500 PB raw, dedupe saves a lot
Changes: ~1k commits/s
data: files: id, path, owner, version, chunk_list
chunks: hash → storage location (deduped)

blocks.c: The desktop client watches folders and splits files into chunks.
blocks.bs: Block service accepts only the chunks that changed.
blocks.mdb: SQL for metadata: versions need strong consistency.
blocks.nt: Other devices are told something changed.
blocks.o: Other devices pull only the new chunks.

dives: Why chunk files?
Upload only changed 4 MB chunks; dedupe identical chunks by hash.
Conflicts?
Version check on commit; on conflict keep both copies.
Why SQL for metadata?
Transactions for versions and paths.
How do devices find out?
Long poll or WebSocket notifications, then fetch changes.
wrap: Bottleneck: metadata DB. Fix: shard by user or namespace.
Next: sharing permissions, LAN sync.

est: Hot event: 1M users for 50k seats in minutes
Normal: low traffic, mostly reads
data: seats: event_id, seat_id, status, UNIQUE (event, seat)
holds in Redis with TTL
bookings: id, user, seats, status

blocks.wr: A virtual waiting room lets people in at a safe rate.
blocks.ev: Event service: details and seat maps.
blocks.bk: Booking service runs hold, pay, confirm.
blocks.lk: Seat holds in Redis with a 10-minute TTL.
blocks.bdb: Bookings in SQL with a unique constraint as the last guard.

dives: How do you prevent double booking?
Hold with SET NX EX in Redis, plus a UNIQUE (event, seat) in the DB.
What happens if payment fails?
The hold expires or is released; the seat returns.
Flash sale?
Waiting room, cached event pages, admit in batches.
Fairness?
Queue position by arrival, block bots.
wrap: Bottleneck: seat-hold contention. Fix: shard holds by section.
Next: resale, dynamic pricing.

reqN: New places can take a day to appear
est: 100M DAU x 5 searches ≈ 6k/s, peaks 30k/s
200M places x 1 KB ≈ 200 GB
data: places: id, name, lat, lng, geohash, category
geo index: geohash cell → place ids

blocks.ls: Location search turns a point into cells and finds places.
blocks.c: Cache of place details for fast results.

dives: How do you search a radius?
Find the geohash cell for the point plus its 8 neighbours, then filter by distance.
Geohash or quadtree?
Geohash is simple; a quadtree adapts to dense cities.
Freshness?
Rebuild the index nightly; edits are rare.
Scale reads?
Replicas and cache; the index fits in memory.
wrap: Bottleneck: dense cells downtown. Fix: longer geohash or quadtree.
Next: ranking by rating and distance.

reqF: Chat with an AI model, answers stream in
Pick the right model for the job
est: 1M DAU x 20 messages ≈ 230 req/s
~1k tokens per turn ≈ 20B tokens/day: cost is the key number
data: conversations, messages (role, content, tokens, model)
usage per user per day

blocks.cs: Chat service streams tokens back over SSE.
blocks.r: The router picks a model by cost and latency.
blocks.sc: Semantic cache answers repeated questions cheaply.
blocks.llm: Hosted model API for the hard questions.
blocks.sh: Self-hosted model for cheap, high volume.
blocks.ob: Tracing and evals: latency, cost, quality.

dives: How do you stream?
Server-Sent Events from the chat service, token by token.
Long conversations?
Trim or summarise old turns to fit the context window.
Cost control?
Route easy prompts to small models, cache, limit tokens per user.
Provider outage?
Fallback to another provider through the router.
wrap: Bottleneck: model latency and cost. Fix: routing, caching, smaller models.
Next: tools, memory, RAG.

reqF: Stay up to date as documents change
reqN: Grounded: say 'not found' instead of guessing
est: 1M documents ≈ 20M chunks x 1.5 KB vectors ≈ 30 GB index
Queries: tens per second
data: chunks: id, doc_id, text, embedding, acl, updated_at
BM25 keyword index alongside vectors

blocks.ch: Load and split into chunks with overlap.
blocks.rag: RAG service runs the pipeline per question.
blocks.rr: A reranker keeps the best 5 of 50.
blocks.llm: The LLM answers from the context, with citations.

dives: Chunk size?
300-800 tokens with overlap; keep source, date and ACL as metadata.
Why hybrid search plus rerank?
Vectors catch meaning, keywords catch exact terms; the reranker orders them.
How do you stop made-up answers?
Answer only from context, cite, say 'not found'.
How do you measure it?
Recall@k for retrieval, faithfulness for answers.
wrap: Bottleneck: retrieval quality. Fix: better chunking, rerank, evals.
Next: agentic RAG, multi-hop questions.

reqF: Ask a human before risky actions
est: A task = 10-50 model calls + tool calls
Long tasks: minutes, so run asynchronously
data: tasks + steps (state, tool calls, results)
memory: vector + key-value

blocks.ag: The orchestrator runs plan, act, observe.
blocks.llm: The model plans the next step.
blocks.mem: Memory to recall and save facts.

dives: How does the loop stop?
Step and token limits, a done check, timeouts.
How do tools stay safe?
Least-privilege permissions, approval for risky ones, sandbox.
Failures mid-task?
Persist state per step, make tools idempotent, resume.
How do you know it works?
Task-success evals and traces.
wrap: Bottleneck: long tasks and cost. Fix: smaller models for sub-steps, caching.
Next: multi-agent, scheduled agents.

reqF: Take a coding task from the terminal or IDE
reqN: Never break the repo: verify before commit
est: A task = 20-100 tool calls
Context is the scarce resource: load only what matters
api: Tool calls: read, edit, grep, shell, git, MCP
data: project memory file loaded every session
session transcript and checkpoints

blocks.ag: The agent loop: gather context, act, verify.
blocks.llm: The model decides the next action.
blocks.sh: Shell sandbox runs tests and builds.
blocks.mcp: MCP servers bring issues and docs.
blocks.git: Commit and open a pull request.

dives: How does it find the right code?
Search first (grep, file tree), then read only what matters.
How do you keep it safe?
Permission modes, sandboxed shell, never push without asking.
How do you know the change works?
Run tests and build before commit.
Big tasks?
Sub-agents search in parallel, each with its own context.
wrap: Bottleneck: context window. Fix: search tools, summaries, sub-agents.
Next: CI integration, code review bots.

reqF: Search the web and internal docs
reqN: Budget on steps, tokens and time
est: One question ≈ 3-6 sub-questions x 10 searches each
Tokens per report: hundreds of thousands
data: plan, sub-questions, findings with source URLs
final report

blocks.u: The user asks a big question.
blocks.w2: Each has its own context window.
blocks.rep: The writer turns findings into a cited report.

dives: Why multiple agents?
Parallel search, separate contexts, faster and broader.
How do findings come back?
Compressed summaries with sources, not raw pages.
How do you control cost?
Budgets on steps, tokens and time per agent.
Quality?
Every claim must cite; check citations before the final report.
wrap: Bottleneck: tokens. Fix: smaller models for search, compression.
Next: follow-up questions, saved research.

reqF: Answer customers from the help centre
reqN: Safe: limits on actions like refunds
est: 10k conversations/day
Target: resolve 50-70% without a human
data: conversations, actions taken, outcome, CSAT

blocks.c: Customers write in by chat or email.
blocks.ag: The support agent decides: answer, act or escalate.
blocks.kb: Answers grounded in the help centre.
blocks.crm: Tools on orders and CRM, with limits.
blocks.h: A human takes over with full context.

dives: How do you keep answers right?
Ground in the help centre with RAG; cite articles.
How do you limit damage?
Tool limits like a refund cap, approval above it.
When to escalate?
Low confidence, angry customer, or asked for a human.
How do you measure it?
Resolution rate, CSAT, escalation rate.
wrap: Bottleneck: hard cases. Fix: better handoff, learn from human replies.
Next: voice channel, proactive messages.

reqF: Talk to callers on the phone or web
Understand and answer in natural speech
est: Latency budget: STT ~200 ms + LLM ~300 ms + TTS ~200 ms + network
Concurrent calls x audio streams
api: SIP / WebRTC audio in and out
Tool calls: book, look up customer
data: call records, transcripts, audio for evals

blocks.rtc: WebRTC or SIP gateway carries audio.
blocks.ag: The voice agent (LLM) decides what to say.

dives: How do you hit 800 ms?
Stream every stage: STT partials, LLM tokens, TTS audio.
Interruptions?
Voice activity detection stops TTS when the caller talks.
Slow tools?
Short filler phrases while the tool runs.
Speech-to-speech models?
Fewer hops and lower latency, less control.
wrap: Bottleneck: latency. Fix: colocate models, stream, smaller models.
Next: multilingual, call analytics.

reqF: One endpoint for every team's model calls
est: Thousands of requests per second across teams
Billions of tokens a month: chargeback matters
data: teams, keys, quotas
usage events: tokens, cost, model, latency

blocks.apps: Internal apps and agents call one gateway.
blocks.g: Guardrails and PII redaction before providers.
blocks.obs: Tracing and cost metering per team.

dives: Why one gateway?
One place for keys, quotas, safety and cost.
Routing?
By cost, latency and capability, with fallback.
Data protection?
Redact PII before it leaves; log what was sent.
Chargeback?
Meter tokens and cost per team key.
wrap: Bottleneck: the gateway itself. Fix: stateless, horizontally scaled.
Next: evals, prompt registry.

reqF: Answer a natural-language question in a few sentences
Ground the answer in fresh web pages
Show 3-6 citations the user can click
Handle follow-up questions in the same thread
reqN: First tokens in about 1-2 s, full answer in a few seconds
Citations must actually support the sentence they sit on
Fresh: news from today should be findable
Cost per answer low enough for a free tier
est: Assume 100M questions/day = ~1,200/s, peaks ~5k/s
Fan-out: 3-8 sub-queries each = ~10-40k searches/s
Retrieve ~100-1,000 candidates, rerank to 5-20 passages
Context: 10 passages x ~300 tokens = ~3k tokens per answer
data: Web index: url, title, passages, crawl_ts, language, authority signals
Inverted index (BM25) + vector index (ANN) over passages
answer log: question, sub_queries, passages_used, citations, model_version

blocks.u: Start from the user's question - it is usually vague or compound.
blocks.rw: An LLM rewrites the question and fans it out into several focused searches (query fan-out).
blocks.web: Gate 1: only pages the crawler indexed can ever be cited.
blocks.kw: BM25 keyword search - wins on exact names, numbers and rare words.
blocks.vx: Vector (ANN) search - wins on meaning and paraphrases.
blocks.fu: Reciprocal Rank Fusion merges both lists without tuning score scales.
blocks.rr: A cross-encoder reranks the top ~100 down to ~10. Gate 3: only these reach the model.
blocks.llm: The LLM writes the answer from the passages in its context window.
blocks.cite: Gate 4: the model picks which passages to cite - the only opaque gate.

dives: Why not just use vector search?
One vector per passage averages away specifics, so exact names and compound queries (X AND Y) get missed. BM25 catches literal matches; fuse both with RRF, then rerank.
Why a two-stage retrieve-then-rerank?
Cheap first stage for recall over millions of passages, expensive cross-encoder only on the top ~100 for precision. Classic cheap structure in front of an expensive operation.
How do you keep citations honest?
Cite at passage level, check each sentence is supported by its cited passage (an entailment check or an LLM judge), and drop citations that fail.
How do you measure quality?
A golden set of questions with judged passages: recall@100 for retrieval, nDCG@10 after rerank, citation precision, and human or LLM-judge answer quality - re-run on every model change.
How do you keep it fresh?
Re-crawl news and high-change pages often, a small fresh index merged at query time, and recency as a ranking feature.
wrap: Bottleneck: reranker latency - cap candidates, distil a smaller reranker, cache popular queries.
Risk: hallucinated or wrong citations - verify support before showing.
Next: personalisation, multimodal answers, shopping results.

reqF: Brands pick prompts (buyer questions) to track
Run every prompt on 5-10 AI engines daily
Detect brand mentions, citations, position, sentiment and competitors
Dashboards, alerts and an API / MCP over the results
reqN: Daily freshness per plan, never double count
Survive provider outages and rate limits
Cost per answer well under 1 cent
Results comparable over time even when engines change
est: 3,000 projects x 300 prompts x 4 engines = 3.6M answers/day = ~40/s avg, spiky
~3 KB per answer = ~10 GB/day raw, ~4 TB/year - S3 is cheap
Pro plan: 100 prompts x 3 engines x 30 days = 9,000 answers/month
Revenue ~$14k/day at $5M ARR -> answers must cost far below 1 cent
Official web-search API fees ~$10-25 per 1,000 calls: 3.6M/day would be $36k+/day before tokens - so dedupe, sample and pick cheaper collection paths
data: Postgres: tenant, project, prompt, engine, plan, quota
run(id, prompt_id, engine, region, model_version, day, run_no) - unique key
S3: raw answer JSON per run (keep forever, re-parse later)
ClickHouse: mention(run_id, brand, cited_url, domain, position, sentiment) ORDER BY (project, day)

blocks.u: Brands and agencies (one agency owns many brands) - multi-tenant from day one.
blocks.app: Web app, public API and MCP server share one service layer.
blocks.pg: Source of truth for tenants, projects, prompts and plan quotas.
blocks.sch: Spreads each project's runs over the day (no thundering herd) and enforces plan quotas.
blocks.q: One queue per engine, so a slow or down engine never blocks the others.
blocks.w: Workers with per-engine rate limits, retries with backoff and a circuit breaker.
blocks.eng: ChatGPT search, Perplexity, AI Overviews, Gemini... each with its own API, limits and quirks.
blocks.raw: Raw answers + citations in S3: cheap, and lets you re-parse when the parser improves.
blocks.p: Rules first (URL -> domain -> brand, alias lists), a small LLM for sentiment and fuzzy matches, schema-checked output.
blocks.ch: Columnar store for millions of facts - dashboards in milliseconds.
blocks.al: Alerts only on real drops (outside the confidence interval) plus a weekly report.
blocks.ev: Hand-labelled golden answers: precision/recall of mention and citation detection on every parser change.

dives: Do the unit economics work?

Search-enabled API calls cost about $10-25 per 1,000. At 3.6M answers/day that is $36k+/day, more than ~$14k/day revenue at $5M ARR. So: share runs across tenants, adaptive sampling, weekly cadence for the long tail, batch pricing for parsing, and compare API vs browser vs data-partner cost per answer.
How do you stop retries double counting?
Idempotent job key = project + prompt + engine + region + day + run number, a unique constraint on run, and upserts into the facts table.
API answers differ from what users see in the app. What do you do?
Be explicit per engine: official API with web search on, headless browser runs from target regions for spot checks, and track the gap as its own metric.
How do you cut cost?
Dedupe identical prompt + engine + region + day across tenants, batch APIs for parsing, rules before LLM, small model for parsing, weekly cadence for long-tail prompts.
How do you parse mentions reliably?
Alias dictionary per brand (names, products, misspellings), URL -> domain -> brand for citations, a small LLM only for ambiguous cases, Zod/Pydantic schema validation, golden-set evals.
Postgres or ClickHouse?
Both: Postgres for config and transactions; ClickHouse for append-only facts with ORDER BY (project, day) and materialized rollups.
wrap: Bottleneck: engine rate limits and cost - quotas, dedupe, adaptive sampling.
Risk: silent parser regressions - golden set in CI, re-parse from raw.
Next: noise-aware scoring, Prompt Universe, agent over the data.

reqF: Turn many noisy AI answers into one visibility score
Show share of voice against competitors
Show how confident the number is
reqN: Statistically honest: no alert on noise
Stable over time across engine updates
Cheap: spend runs only where they matter
Explainable to a marketer in one line
est: Answers vary run to run: 1 run per prompt is not enough
10 runs at 7 mentions -> 70% with a 95% interval of roughly 40-89% (Wilson)
More runs shrink the interval roughly with the square root of N
300 prompts x 4 engines x 5 runs = 6,000 answers per project per day
data: fact(run_id, prompt, engine, brand, mentioned, cited, position)
daily_rollup(project, prompt, engine, day, n, mentions, cites)
engine_event(engine, ts, kind: model_update | search_toggle)

blocks.pr: Each tracked question plus a few phrasings - one wording is a biased sample.
blocks.r: Run each prompt N times per engine and region: the unit of measure is a run.
blocks.eng: Non-deterministic: the same prompt 30 seconds apart can give a different answer.
blocks.f: Per-run facts: mentioned? cited? at what position?
blocks.st: Rate = mentions / runs, with a Wilson interval (works at small N, unlike the plain +/- formula).
blocks.sov: Score and Share of Voice shown as a range: '7 of 10 runs (45-90%)'.
blocks.an: Flags a change only when the new rate falls outside last period's interval.
blocks.mv: Engine model updates and search toggles are annotations - a jump may be the engine, not the brand.
blocks.ad: Adaptive sampling: more runs where variance is high or a decision is close, fewer where it is stable.

dives: Why not just show the latest answer?
Answers are random samples. One run tells you almost nothing; a rate over N runs with an interval tells you what users usually see.
Why Wilson and not mean +/- 2 standard errors?
At small N and rates near 0% or 100% the simple formula gives impossible ranges (below 0). Wilson stays inside 0-100% and is honest at small N.
How do you detect a real drop?
Compare this week's interval with last week's (or a two-proportion test), require a minimum N, and use rolling windows to smooth daily noise.
How do you control cost?
Adaptive sampling - stop early when the interval is already narrow, add runs only where the interval straddles a decision threshold.
An engine ships a new model. Now what?
Annotate the timeline, compare before/after on a fixed control prompt set, and avoid alerting customers on an engine-wide shift.
wrap: Risk: false alarms erode trust - alert on significance, not on movement.
Next: weight prompts by demand so the score reflects real buyer traffic.
Next: per-engine and per-region breakdowns with the same interval logic.

reqF: Suggest the buyer questions a brand should track
Weight topics by how often people ask
reqN: Results in minutes for a new brand
Stable topic ids so trends don't reset
est: Generate ~5,000 candidate questions per brand, keep ~300
Embeddings: 5,000 x 1,536 dims x 4 bytes = ~30 MB per brand
Clustering 5k vectors takes seconds on one machine
Re-cluster monthly, add new questions weekly
data: candidate(id, text, source, embedding, locale)
topic(id, label, centroid, weight, parent_ids[])
Vector index over prompts with filters: tenant, locale, topic

blocks.src: Inputs: the brand's site, search-console keywords and competitors.
blocks.gen: An LLM writes many realistic buyer questions per product and persona.
blocks.fo: Captures the hidden sub-queries engines fan out to - they show what really gets searched.
blocks.emb: Turns every question into a vector so similar meaning sits close together.
blocks.cl: Clusters questions into topics and drops near-duplicates above a similarity threshold.
blocks.dm: Demand signals (search volume, Bing AI grounding topics) weight each topic.
blocks.vx: Vector index over prompts, filtered by tenant and locale, for search and dedupe.
blocks.set: One representative prompt per cluster, weighted by demand.
blocks.rv: A marketer approves or edits before anything is tracked (and paid for).

dives: How do you pick the similarity threshold?
Label a few hundred pairs as same/different question, sweep the threshold, and pick the point with the best precision for 'duplicate' - measure, don't guess.
Why not a strict topic tree?
Real taxonomies are multi-parent (a question can be about pricing AND integrations), so store topics as tags with parent_ids, not one folder.
How do you keep topic ids stable after re-clustering?
Match new clusters to old ones by centroid similarity and keep the old id when the match is strong.
How do you search prompts for a brand name?
Hybrid: BM25 for exact brand and product names, vectors for meaning, fused with RRF.
wrap: Risk: generated questions nobody really asks - weight by demand signals.
Next: per-locale universes and competitor gap analysis.
Next: feed winning topics into Content Studio.

reqF: Answer 'why did our visibility drop last week?' in chat
Show the evidence: example answers and cited pages
Expose the same tools to customers' own agents via MCP
reqN: Answers grounded in real numbers, not guesses
Fast: a few seconds per turn
est: Say 10k agent conversations/day, ~6 tool calls each = 60k tool calls/day
Batched tool calls cut turns roughly in half (fewer LLM round trips)
Each turn ~5-15k tokens of context
Read-only by default: writes need approval
api: Tools: get_visibility(project, engine, range), top_citations(project, topic), compare(brands[]), sample_answers(prompt, n)
MCP server: same tools, OAuth / API key, per-key scopes and rate limits
data: Facts in ClickHouse, raw answers in S3
trace(run_id, tool_calls[], tokens, latency, eval_scores)
skills: versioned playbooks (markdown + tool recipes)

blocks.u: A marketer asks a question in plain English.
blocks.ext: Customers' own agents (Claude, ChatGPT) call the same tools over MCP.
blocks.mcp: MCP server: API keys, scopes, rate limits - the tool layer as a product.
blocks.ag: The agent loop with plan mode: plan, call tools, check, answer.
blocks.llm: The model that plans and writes - small model for simple steps, larger for analysis.
blocks.sk: Skills: reusable playbooks ('diagnose a drop') loaded only when relevant.
blocks.t: Fixed, typed metric tools rather than free text-to-SQL - safer and testable.
blocks.g: Guardrails: tenant id injected by the server, row filters, read-only by default.
blocks.raw: Example answers and cited pages as evidence links.
blocks.tr: Traces of every run plus an eval set of real questions with expected answers.

dives: Text-to-SQL or fixed tools?
Start with fixed, typed tools for the top questions (safe, fast, testable); add text-to-SQL later behind a read-only role, tenant row filters and query limits.
How do you guarantee tenant isolation?
The model never chooses the tenant: the server injects tenant_id into every tool call, and the database enforces row-level filters as a second line.
How do you make it faster and cheaper?
Let the model batch several tool calls in one turn (fan-out), cache tool results per day, and route simple steps to a small model.
How do you evaluate the agent?
A set of real questions with expected findings, trace every run, check tool choice (did it call the right tools?) and answer correctness, and re-run on every model or prompt change.
Tool selection with 50+ tools?
It's a retrieval problem: describe tools well, retrieve the top few per request (or group them into skills), and measure tool-selection recall.
wrap: Risk: confident wrong answers - require evidence links for every claim.
Risk: prompt injection from cited web pages - treat page text as data, never as instructions.
Next: scheduled agent runs that send a weekly 'what changed and why'.

reqF: Show which pages AI crawlers read and how often
Tell real AI bots from fakes
Link AI crawling to AI referral traffic and conversions
reqN: Ingest millions of log lines per day per big site
Dashboards load in under a second
No PII stored from human visitors
est: A busy site: 50M hits/day = ~600/s, maybe 5-20% bots
Raw log line ~500 B -> 25 GB/day per big customer before compression
Columnar compression ~10x -> ~2.5 GB/day
Rollup page x bot x day turns billions of rows into millions
api: Log push endpoint (Cloudflare / Vercel / Fastly) or an edge snippet
data: hit(ts, project, url, bot, verified, status, bytes) ORDER BY (project, ts)
Materialized view: page x bot x day counts
bot_ranges(bot, cidr, fetched_at) refreshed daily

blocks.bots: AI crawlers (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot) and humans hit the site.
blocks.cdn: The CDN or edge pushes logs - no code change on the customer's site.
blocks.k: Kafka buffers raw hits so spikes never drop data.
blocks.v: Verify bots: user agent is easy to fake, so also check published IP ranges or reverse DNS.
blocks.ip: Bot operators publish IP ranges - refresh them daily.
blocks.ch: ClickHouse stores hits in big batched inserts.
blocks.ga: GA4 / Search Console referrals from chatgpt.com or perplexity.ai show traffic coming back.
blocks.mv: Materialized views keep page x bot x day counts up to date as data arrives.

dives: How do you verify a bot is really GPTBot?
Match the user agent, then check the IP against the operator's published ranges (or reverse DNS then forward DNS). Mark unverified hits separately.
Why ClickHouse and not Postgres?
Billions of append-only rows and aggregate queries: columnar storage reads only the columns needed and compresses well; Postgres row storage would scan far more.
How do you join crawling to revenue?
Referrer = AI engine -> session -> conversion in GA4; show crawl-to-referral ratios per page.
Privacy?
Keep bot hits in full, sample or aggregate human hits, drop IPs of humans after bot detection.
wrap: Bottleneck: ingest bursts - Kafka buffer + batch inserts.
Next: alert when a key page stops being crawled.
Next: recommend robots.txt / llms.txt changes.

reqF: Serve clean markdown to AI crawlers, HTML to humans
Publish llms.txt and an alternate link
No drift between the two versions
reqN: No impact on human page speed
Cheap to run at the edge
est: HTML page ~177 KB vs markdown ~4 KB (~97% smaller)
Bots are a small share of hits but read many pages
Edge middleware adds ~1 ms per request
Thousands of pages: build markdown at deploy time
api: Middleware: if verified AI bot -> rewrite to /api/md/[...path]
data: Per page: MDX source + optional colocated machine.md
Fallback: generated markdown stripped from the MDX
Cache key includes a bot/human flag

blocks.h: A normal visitor gets the full HTML page.
blocks.bot: An AI crawler gets a markdown version of the same page.
blocks.mw: Edge middleware checks the user agent (and ideally verifies the IP) before deciding.
blocks.md: A rewrite (not a redirect), so the URL - and any citation - stays the real page.
blocks.cache: The CDN cache key must vary on bot vs human, or humans could be served markdown.
blocks.src: One source of truth: MDX plus an optional hand-written machine.md.
blocks.llms: llms.txt and an alternate link tell crawlers where the markdown lives.
blocks.ci: A CI check fails the build if markdown and HTML drift apart.

dives: Why rewrite and not redirect?
A redirect changes the URL the crawler records; a rewrite keeps the canonical URL, so citations point to the real page.
Isn't this cloaking?
Not if the content is equivalent - same facts, cleaner format. A CI diff check keeps it honest.
How do you prove it helps?
A/B by page groups: half the pages dual-served, half not, compare crawl rate and citation rate over weeks with the noise-aware score.
What breaks with caching?
If the cache key ignores bot vs human, the first visitor type poisons the cache. Add the flag to the key or send Vary on the header you switch on.
wrap: Risk: fake bots - verify by IP ranges.
Risk: drift - generate from one source.
Next: structured data (schema.org) in both versions.

reqF: Crawl a brand's whole site on demand and on a schedule
Check structure: schema markup, headings, liftable facts
reqN: Polite: never overload a customer's site
Finishes a 10k-page site in under an hour
est: 10k pages at 2-5 requests/s per domain = ~35-80 minutes
Raw HTML ~100 KB x 10k = ~1 GB per crawl
Headless rendering ~10x more expensive than a plain fetch
1,000 sites re-crawled weekly = ~10M fetches/week
data: frontier(domain, url, priority, next_fetch_at)
page(url, hash, etag, last_modified, fetched_at)
finding(audit_id, url, check, severity, fix)

blocks.start: An audit request names the domain.
blocks.fr: Crawl frontier with one queue per domain - the simplest way to stay polite.
blocks.rb: Respect robots.txt and use sitemaps to find pages fast.
blocks.f: Fetchers with a per-domain rate limit and backoff on errors.
blocks.js: Render with a headless browser only when the raw HTML is empty (JS sites).
blocks.dd: Normalise URLs and use a Bloom filter for 'seen this URL?' plus content hashes for duplicate pages.
blocks.chk: Checks: schema markup, headings, AI bot access, page structure.
blocks.llm: A small LLM flags whether key facts are stated in clear, liftable sentences.
blocks.pg: Findings plus last-crawl data (ETag, hash) for the next incremental crawl.
blocks.fix: Findings become fix suggestions and content tasks.

dives: How do you stay polite?
One queue per domain, a per-domain rate limit, honour Crawl-delay and 429/503 with backoff, and crawl off-peak.
Why a Bloom filter?
Tiny memory for 'have I seen this URL?' - it can say 'maybe seen' by mistake (rarely skipping a page) but never misses one it has truly seen.
How do you re-crawl cheaply?
Conditional GETs with ETag / If-Modified-Since, sitemap lastmod, and content hashes to skip unchanged pages.
When do you render JavaScript?
Only when the raw HTML is missing the main content - rendering costs about 10x a plain fetch.
wrap: Bottleneck: headless rendering - pool browsers, render only when needed.
Next: track fixes over time and link them to visibility changes.
Next: a crawl budget per plan.

reqF: Tell whether a new ranker is better before shipping
Cover real user queries, including rare ones
Explain why a query got worse
reqN: Trustworthy: metrics agree with human judgement
Fast enough to run on every change
est: Golden set: a few hundred to a few thousand real queries
Graded labels (0-3) on the top ~20 results per query
Interleaving detects ranking differences with far less traffic than A/B
One offline run = queries x rankers, minutes on a laptop
data: query(id, text, source, frequency)
judgment(query_id, doc_id, grade 0-3, rater, ts)
eval_run(id, ranker_version, metrics, per_query_scores)

blocks.q: Sample real queries, not invented ones - head and long tail.
blocks.gs: The golden set: queries with graded judgments of which results are relevant.
blocks.hj: Domain experts label first; their labels define 'right'.
blocks.jd: An LLM judge scales labelling - only after it agrees with the humans.
blocks.run: Runs old and new rankers on the same queries.
blocks.met: recall@100 for the first stage, nDCG@10 for the final order, MRR when one answer matters.
blocks.ab: Online check: interleaving (mix both rankers' results, see which gets clicks) or a full A/B test.
blocks.ci: A CI gate blocks merges that drop the metrics.
blocks.err: Read the worst queries by hand - that is where the next fix comes from.

dives: Why nDCG and not accuracy?
Ranking quality depends on order and graded relevance; nDCG rewards putting the best results first and discounts lower positions.
recall@100 vs nDCG@10 - which when?
recall@100 for the first-stage retriever (did the right docs make the candidate pool?), nDCG@10 after the reranker (is the top in the right order?).
How do you trust an LLM judge?
Label ~100 items with experts, measure the judge's agreement (true positive and true negative rates), fix the rubric until it agrees, then re-check on every judge model change.
Interleaving or A/B?
Interleaving for ranking comparisons - each user sees a mix, so it needs much less traffic; A/B for business metrics like conversion.
wrap: Risk: overfitting to the golden set - refresh it with new queries.
Next: per-segment metrics (locale, query type).
Next: track cost per query next to quality.

reqF: Answer complex questions needing several searches
Use several tools: keyword, vector, web, SQL
Decide when enough evidence is found
reqN: Bounded cost and latency per question
High recall of the needed evidence
est: Classic tool calling: one search per turn, many turns
Batching searches in one turn cuts turns roughly 2-3x
Each turn re-sends context: fewer turns = fewer tokens
Cap: e.g. 5 turns, 40k tokens per question
api: Tools: search_keyword(q, k), search_vector(q, k, filter), web(q), sql(query)
data: trace(question, plan, tool_calls[], passages, judge_verdicts, tokens)
Eval set: question -> required evidence ids
Cache: tool results per (tool, args) for the session

blocks.u: A compound question - needs more than one search.
blocks.pl: The planner splits it into sub-queries and picks tools.
blocks.cm: Code mode: the model writes one small script that fires many searches at once.
blocks.s1: Keyword search for names, ids and exact phrases.
blocks.s3: Web search or SQL for fresh facts and numbers.
blocks.ctx: Context packing is ranking: dedupe, rank, truncate to the budget.
blocks.jg: The judge decides: enough evidence, or refine and search again.
blocks.ans: The final answer, every claim tied to a citation.

dives: Why batch tool calls?
Each turn re-sends the whole context. Fanning out several searches in one turn (or one script) cuts turns, tokens and latency while raising recall.
How does the agent know when to stop?
A judge step checks coverage of each sub-question, plus hard caps on turns and tokens; stop early when every sub-question has strong evidence.
How do you evaluate it?
Questions with known required evidence: measure evidence recall, answer correctness, turns and cost per question - on every model or prompt change.
Tool selection with many tools?
Treat it as retrieval: retrieve the few relevant tools per request, measure tool-selection recall.
wrap: Risk: runaway loops - caps and a budget per question.
Risk: injected instructions in fetched pages - treat as data.
Next: learn from traces which plans work.

reqF: Merge an acquired company's data pipeline into yours
reqN: No silent metric jumps for customers
Cost of running both is time-boxed
est: Dual run for 2-4 weeks doubles collection cost for migrated tenants
Compare thousands of metrics per tenant per day
Define tolerance up front, e.g. visibility within the confidence interval
Backfill: re-parse months of raw answers with the new parser
data: mapping(old_id, new_id, kind: brand | prompt | project)
diff(tenant, metric, day, old, new, within_tolerance)
cutover(tenant, ts, by) shown as a chart annotation

blocks.src: Feed both pipelines exactly the same prompts and engines.
blocks.a: The acquired pipeline keeps running as the reference.
blocks.b: Your pipeline runs in shadow on the same inputs.
blocks.map: A mapping table translates ids, brand names and prompts between the two worlds.
blocks.rec: The reconciler diffs metrics per tenant and checks them against agreed tolerances.
blocks.bf: Backfill: re-parse history with the new parser so trends line up.
blocks.sw: Cut over tenant by tenant behind a flag, with a quick rollback.

dives: How do you decide the new pipeline is 'the same'?
Agree tolerances per metric up front (inside the confidence interval for noisy rates, exact for counts), then require N clean days before cutover.
The numbers differ. Who is right?
Inspect sampled raw answers from both, labelled by hand - the golden set decides, not either pipeline.
How do you avoid a cliff in customers' charts?
Backfill history with the new parser, annotate the cutover date, and explain any method change in the product.
wrap: Risk: double cost - time-box the dual run.
Risk: hidden differences in prompts or regions - log every input.
Next: delete the old pipeline and its data per retention rules.
